On the left side is the power supply E, and the lower left side has internal resistance R0 connected in series; at the top there is a variable resistor R1 with an oblique arrow; on the right side there is resistor R2; these elements are connected in sequence in the same closed loop, so R0, R1, R2 and power supply E form a series loop. The loop current I = E / (R1 + a) = 10 / (R1 + 2.5). The power obtained on R1 is P1 = I^2 R1 = 100 R1 / (R1 + 2.5)^2. For the function x/(x+a)^2, it takes the maximum value when x = a, so the maximum power occurs at R1 = 2.5 Ω. At this time Pmax = 100 × 2.5 / (2.5 + 2.5)^2 = 250 / 25 = 10 W.

method.method_draft: From the image, identify R0, R1, and R2 as series elements with the source E. From the text, substitute E=10 V, R0=0.5 ohm, and R2=2 ohm. Let a=R0+R2=2.5 ohm. The current is I=E/(a+R1), so the power in the variable resistor is P1=I^2 R1=100 R1/(R1+2.5)^2. Differentiate with respect to R1, or use the known maximum of x/(x+a)^2, to find the maximum occurs at R1=a=2.5 ohm. Then Pmax=100*2.5/(5)^2=10 W.

method.method_draft: From the image, remove the top variable resistor R1 and view the rest of the circuit from R1's two terminals. With R1 open, no current flows, so there is no voltage drop across R0 or R2; hence the Thevenin voltage across the R1 terminals is Vth=E=10 V. To find Thevenin resistance, replace the ideal voltage source by a short; the resistance seen between the R1 terminals is Rth=R0+R2=0.5+2=2.5 ohm. By maximum power transfer, set R1=Rth, and compute Pmax=Vth^2/(4Rth)=100/(4*2.5)=10 W.
